clue.text: A ball for the complete cast

parts.note: complete means full
to cast is to toss or throw

explanation.surface: A cricket delivery suited to someone who throws with everything they have.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a FULL TOSS is a ball that reaches the batsman without bouncing.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket this is a delivery that arrives at the batsman without pitching first.

clue.text: The yarns, or lies, accepts again

indicators.note: one word accepting another takes it inside itself, so the word for lies holds the piece

parts.note: small lies are fibs
RE is a prefix meaning again

explanation.surface: Someone telling stories, or untruths, takes them on board a second time.
explanation.definitionFit: Yarns are threads, which are fibres spun together for weaving.

clue.text: Rested the hoop against the shed

parts.note: rested (against something) means leant
a hoop is round, the shape of the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone propped a child's hoop up against the garden shed.
explanation.definitionFit: A lean-to is a small shed built against the wall of a larger building.

clue.text: Understanding to be deceiving

definitions.meaning: taking something in is grasping or understanding it
taking someone in is fooling or deceiving them

explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb has two senses: to absorb mentally, and to dupe someone.

clue.text: Gives one's word to

parts.note: read as making a promise to someone, but it simply means utters or states

explanation.definitionFit: To give a word is to utter it, so someone doing that states or speaks it.

clue.text: Going back to hold under water, is very nasty to

indicators.note: going back tells us to read the whole assembled piece from right to left
the word for water is to hold the word for under inside itself

parts.note: the sea is a body of water
SUB is Latin and a prefix for under

explanation.surface: A bully keeps pushing someone's head under the water in a nasty prank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going back' turns the whole SESUBA assembly round; the comma hides that 'is' belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To abuse someone is to treat them cruelly, which is being very nasty to them.

clue.text: Ice-creams? Everybody loves them

parts.note: blocks of ice cream are sold under this name, and an old phrase calls a dependable good person by the same word

explanation.walkthrough: In dated British slang a kind, reliable person is 'a brick', so everybody loves them.
explanation.definitionFit: Ice cream is sold in rectangular blocks of that name, and a reliable friend is called one in old British slang.

clue.text: Support, as usual

definitions.meaning: an upright pole or post that supports something

explanation.definitionFit: A standard is an upright support such as a lamp standard, and the adjective means normal or customary.

clue.text: Ram home?

parts.note: reads as forcing a point home, but a ram is a male sheep and its home is an enclosure

explanation.definitionFit: A pen is an enclosure where sheep, including the male ram, are kept.

clue.text: Would the servant be concealing evidence of a fight?

indicators.note: the word be is concealing the servant word inside it, between its two letters

parts.note: a lackey is a servant

explanation.surface: A question about whether a footman is covering up after a brawl.
explanation.definitionFit: A bruised eye is the classic mark left on someone after a punch-up.

clue.text: Fantasy I tease myself about

indicators.note: myself goes about, or around, the other pieces

parts.note: myself is me
to rag is to tease

explanation.surface: Someone admits to a daydream in which they make fun of themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: A mirage is an illusion, something imagined that is not really there, like a fantasy.

clue.text: Said by the sergeant-major, it doesn't mean 'Fire!'

definitions.text: Said by the sergeant-major, it doesn't mean 'Fire!'

parts.words: Said by the sergeant-major, it doesn't mean 'Fire!'
parts.note: a parade-ground order to break ranks, which elsewhere could mean sacking someone, but here does not

explanation.definitionFit: The order dismissing a parade sends soldiers away; in an office the same word would mean firing someone.

clue.text: Measure the old marquee

parts.note: ex means former or old
a marquee is a large tent

explanation.surface: Someone sizes up the old marquee before a garden party.
explanation.definitionFit: Extent is the size or scope of something, its measure.

clue.text: Rescued after the shipwreck, one learned

definitions.meaning: survivors of a wreck are collected from the water by rescuers
to learn something casually is to acquire it informally

explanation.definitionFit: Survivors are collected by a rescue boat, and a skill acquired casually is said to be acquired that way.

clue.text: Do they waken one up with their shouting?

definitions.text: Do they waken one up with their shouting?

parts.words: Do they waken one up with their shouting?
parts.note: suggests people who shout to rouse a sleeper, but describes visitors who come to the door

explanation.definitionFit: Visitors who drop in at a house are known by this name, as are people who shout.

clue.text: Wins the confidence of the said foolish Mrs Turner

indicators.note: foolish suggests letters behaving in a silly, disordered way

explanation.surface: Someone charms a scatterbrained woman named Mrs Turner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'foolish' rearranges SAID and MRS; 'Turner' just completes the name, though it hints at turning too.
explanation.definitionFit: To disarm someone is to win them over by charm, gaining their trust.

clue.text: Having taken right into charge, let go

indicators.note: into tells us the letter for right goes inside the other word

parts.note: a fee is a charge

explanation.surface: After taking the right person into custody, the police released them.
explanation.definitionFit: To free a prisoner is to release them, letting them go.

clue.text: Seals and posts

definitions.meaning: an envelope is closed by gumming its flap down
to post a notice is to pin it on a board

explanation.definitionFit: Gumming an envelope shut and pinning a notice to a board are both described by this phrasal verb.

clue.text: Left at home if a member of the family is about

indicators.note: the family member is about, or around, the at-home word

parts.note: a sister is a family member
in means at home

explanation.surface: Someone is told to leave home if a particular relative is around.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinister is Latin for left and is used for the left side in heraldry.

clue.text: Earned-or nicked

definitions.meaning: arrested by the police, in British slang

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both bringing in money as earnings and, in British slang, being arrested by police.

clue.text: Follow to the end

definitions.meaning: to follow someone secretly is to shadow them
the rear part or end of something

explanation.definitionFit: A detective shadows a suspect, and the hindmost part of an animal or a queue has the same name.

clue.text: A great picture!

parts.note: sounds like praise for a fine film, but describes a photograph taken at very short range, making the subject look large

explanation.definitionFit: A shot taken at close range shows its subject large in the frame.

clue.text: A drink that's lacking in body?

definitions.meaning: a ghost or soul has no physical body

explanation.definitionFit: Distilled liquor such as gin is a spirit, and a disembodied ghost is one too.

clue.text: Stamping grounds of the cockney members of the family

indicators.note: a cockney speaker drops the initial h, so the pronunciation matches the family word

parts.note: aunts are family members

explanation.surface: Asks where a Londoner's relatives like to spend their time.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockneys (working-class East Londoners) traditionally drop the h at the start of words.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone's haunts are the places they often visit, their stamping grounds.

clue.text: Seen to have got into someone's clutches

definitions.meaning: past participle of behold, meaning looked at

definitions.text: to have got into someone's clutches
definitions.meaning: split in two, the word means to be gripped by somebody

explanation.definitionFit: The past participle of behold means seen, and split as two words it means gripped.

clue.text: The vessels that are docking?

parts.note: suggests ships arriving in port, but docking also means cutting short, as shears or hair trimmers do

explanation.definitionFit: These are both fast sailing ships and tools for trimming or cutting things short.

clue.text: Verbal excuses, if you don't mind

indicators.note: verbal means spoken, so the word is said out loud

parts.note: pleas are excuses offered in defence

explanation.surface: Asking politely to hear someone's spoken excuses.
explanation.definitionFit: This polite word is used to make a request courteously, like saying if you don't mind.

clue.text: Blow the report!

definitions.meaning: the loud noise of a gun firing

explanation.definitionFit: A heavy knock and the sound of a gunshot share this short word.

clue.text: Work that was the rage of the day

parts.note: Sat is the abbreviation for Saturday
ire is anger or rage

explanation.surface: A piece of writing that was all the fashion in its time.
explanation.definitionFit: A satire is a literary or dramatic work that mocks its subject.

clue.text: I'm sorry father is against modern innovations

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father

indicators.note: innovations are new arrangements, so the letters of modern are made over

explanation.surface: A father apologises for disliking new-fangled ideas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'innovations' makes RDONME; 'is against' only means next to, so it is a link and not the word ON.
explanation.definitionFit: This phrase is a polite apology, said just as one would say sorry.

clue.text: Do I get included in the equality?

indicators.note: the letter is to be put inside the word for a do

parts.note: a do is a party

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether they count as an equal.
explanation.definitionFit: Parity means being equal in status or amount.

clue.text: Is, on being cast into the old prison, tortured

indicators.note: into tells us the cast letters go inside the word for old

parts.note: aged means old

indicators.note: cast suggests the letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A prisoner thrown into an ancient jail suffers torment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being cast' makes ONIS; 'prison' merely dresses the scene, and 'the old' is not GAOL.
explanation.definitionFit: Agonised means in great pain or torment, as if tortured.
